topic: Law fact / myth-buster: 'digital arrest' is a scam - police, CBI, ED, customs or judges do not arrest anyone on a video call (I4C advisory); Supreme Court (29 Oct 2026, suo motu digital arrest case, CJI Surya Kant, Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana) says RBI rules must make banks compensate victims where the bank's lack of due diligence enabled the fraud; report at 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in

slides.title: No one can arrest you on a **video call**
slides.subtitle: Three myths about **"digital arrest"** scams, and what the Supreme Court said on 29 October 2026.
slides.cite: **Supreme Court suo motu case on digital arrest scams** · CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V. Mohana · Hearing of 29 Oct 2026

slides.label: Myth 1
slides.title: "Police can arrest me **on a call**"
bullets: **Fact:** the government's Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) says CBI, police, customs, ED or judges **do not** arrest anyone on a video call.
"Digital arrest" is a **scam**. The caller only wants your money.
The Chief Justice asked who in a democracy believes they can be arrested on a mobile. **Hang up** and the "arrest" is over.

slides.label: Myth 2
slides.title: "The bank owes me **nothing**"
bullets: **Fact:** the Supreme Court said the RBI's new rules must make banks **compensate** victims where weak safeguards or lack of **due diligence** helped the fraud.
The order says compensation should be **not less than** the amount the customer lost.
The bank itself should be liable, not only one employee.
slides.note: **Law fact:** the court wants banks to **pause** unusual transactions, alert the police and verify them before the money moves.

slides.label: Myth 3
slides.title: "Reporting **won't help**"
bullets: **Fact:** I4C asks victims to report at once on the cybercrime helpline **1930** or at **cybercrime.gov.in**.
The Chief Justice also urged victims to go to the **police**.
Scammers may show **fake court orders**. The case that started this matter involved forged judicial orders.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Compensation is **not automatic** yet
bullets: RBI is to notify its new rules by **30 November** and bring them into force by **31 December 2026**. The court will review them.
The bank's liability depends on its **failure** of due diligence.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

slides.title: Know the law, know your **rights**

caption:
Got a video call saying you are under "digital arrest"? It is a scam. Hang up 📵⚖️

Myth 1: "Police can arrest me on a call." No. The government's Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has made it clear that CBI, police, customs, ED or judges do not arrest anyone on a video call. On 29 October 2026, the Chief Justice of India asked who, in a democracy, believes they can be arrested on a mobile phone.

Myth 2: "If I lose money, the bank owes me nothing." Not necessarily. The Supreme Court has said the RBI's new rules must make banks compensate victims where weak safeguards or the bank's lack of due diligence helped the fraud, and the compensation should not be less than the amount lost. The court also wants banks to pause unusual transactions, alert the police and verify them first. These rules are still being framed: RBI is to notify them by 30 November and bring them into force by 31 December 2026.

Myth 3: "Reporting won't help." Report at once on the national cybercrime helpline 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in, and go to your local police station. Remember, scammers may show fake court orders; the case that started this matter involved forged judicial orders.

Case: Suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams, Supreme Court of India (hearing of 29 Oct 2026)
Bench: CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana

This post is for information only, not legal advice.
